cited_evidence.text: In this study, we delved into the enhanced ductility and strength of the FeCoCrNiMo5−xCx-based medium-entropy alloy at cryogenic temperatures. Moreover, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the impact of carbides on the properties of the alloy. For the Mo5 and Mo4C1 alloys, yield strength and tensile strength showed a notable improvement when the temperatures were reduced to 77 K and 4.2 K. This improvement can be associated with the increased critical shear stress for plastic deformation and the resistance from the dislocation interactions under cryogenic conditions. It is clearly shown that the yield strength at cryogenic temperatures significantly surpasses the yield strength at ambient temperature. The results reveal that at reduced temperatures, deformation-induced twinning and martensitic transformation mechanisms are activated, significantly enhancing the work-hardening effects observable in the tensile engineering stress–strain curves. The dynamic Hall–Petch effect, which is attributable to twinning during deformation, is believed to be the underlying reason for the observed strain-hardening mechanics in the alloy.

cited_evidence.text: The quasi-static compressive stress–strain curves of the alloys with varying W contents are presented in Figure 2a. For the W0 alloy, the yield strength (σYS) and the ultimate strength (σUS) are approximately 1620 MPa and 1810 MPa, respectively, with an elongation of ~22%. Serrated steps observed in the stress–strain curve of W0 suggest a susceptibility to plastic instability. The introduction of W into the alloy preserves the high yield strength while significantly improving both fracture strength and fracture strain []. For example, the W13 alloy demonstrates a yield strength of 1650 MPa, along with an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa and a fracture strain of 32%. Figure 2b presents the dynamic engineering stress–strain curves of alloys with varying W contents, tested at high strain rates (2000 s−1) and at room temperature. Under dynamic conditions, the yield strength of each alloy is significantly enhanced compared with the quasi-static conditions. Notably, while the W0 and W8 alloys exhibit poor dynamic plasticity with elongations below 10%, the W13 and W18 alloys demonstrate superior dynamic mechanical properties, achieving ultra-high dynamic yield strengths (exceeding 2200 MPa)

decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has shown that these materials can exhibit exceptional mechanical properties, including high strength, ductility, and resistance to deformation. However, their behavior under dynamic loading conditions, such as high strain rates, is not well understood. Recent studies have investigated the effects of strain rate on the mechanical properties of various high-entropy alloys, including the HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy. These studies have shown that the yield strength and compressive strength of these alloys can increase with increasing strain rate, but the ductility and uniform deformability can decrease. The formation of twins, dislocation density, and grain size have been identified as key factors influencing the mechanical behavior of high-entropy alloys under dynamic loading conditions.
decision.unsolved: The limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure of the HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy under adiabatic dynamic deformation remain unsolved. The exact mechanisms underlying these limitations are not fully understood, and further research is needed to develop strategies to overcome them.
decision.why: Grain refinement has been shown to improve the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys, including their strength, ductility, and resistance to deformation. By reducing the grain size, the formation of twins and dislocation density can be increased, leading to enhanced strain hardening and uniform deformability. Furthermore, grain refinement can help to reduce the adiabatic heating effects that can occur during dynamic deformation, thereby improving the overall mechanical behavior of the alloy.
